question: Marie Curie's handwritten lab notebooks from the 1890s are stored in lead-lined boxes in Paris, and readers must sign a waiver before touching them. What is the problem with these notebooks?
source_excerpt: Marie Curie's Research Papers Are Still Radioactive a Century Later

extra.why_interesting: Players picture a paper notebook as harmless; the reveal is that a 130-year-old document is still dangerous because of the work it records.
extra.verification_notes: Curie's notebooks are contaminated with radium-226 (half-life ~1,600 years), kept in lead-lined boxes at the BnF, and still radioactive; no newer development changes this.

explanation: Curie handled radium and polonium with her bare hands, and the contamination on her papers will stay dangerous for well over a thousand years.

question: Albert Einstein received his only Nobel Prize in 1921, and the citation deliberately did not mention relativity. Which effect, involving light knocking electrons out of metal, was he honoured for explaining?
source_excerpt: for his services to Theoretical Physics, and especially for his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect

extra.why_interesting: Everyone associates Einstein with relativity, yet the Nobel committee pointedly avoided it and cited a different piece of work.
extra.verification_notes: Einstein's 1921 Physics prize (awarded 1922) cited the law of the photoelectric effect and not relativity, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Einstein.

explanation: The committee considered relativity too controversial and unproven, so it rewarded Einstein's 1905 explanation of the photoelectric effect, a cornerstone of quantum theory.

question: The fortune that pays for the Nobel Prizes, including the Peace Prize, came mostly from Alfred Nobel's 1867 patent for which invention?
source_excerpt: Nobel patented dynamite in 1867, a substance easier and safer to handle than the more unstable nitroglycerin.

extra.why_interesting: The world's most prestigious peace prize is paid for by an explosive, a contrast many players have never put together.
extra.verification_notes: Nobel patented dynamite in 1867, and it is the standard answer for the source of his fortune, though his wealth also drew on wider explosives businesses and oil investments (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Nobel).

explanation: Nobel stabilised nitroglycerin by soaking it into an absorbent earth, and the resulting dynamite made him one of Europe's richest men.

question: Five of the Nobel Prizes are handed out in Stockholm every December. The Peace Prize is presented the same day in a different capital city. Which one?
source_excerpt: The Nobel Peace Prize is presented separately in Oslo, Norway. The ceremony has been held at Oslo City Hall since 1990.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume all Nobels are Swedish; the Peace Prize ceremony is actually in a different country, as Nobel's own will specified.
extra.verification_notes: The Peace Prize is presented in Oslo on December 10 while the other five prizes are presented in Stockholm; no newer venue change found (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize).

explanation: Alfred Nobel's will gave the Peace Prize to a Norwegian committee, at a time when Norway and Sweden were still joined in a union.

question: The economics prize is not in Alfred Nobel's will; it was added later by Sweden's central bank. In which year was it awarded for the first time?
source_excerpt: first awarded in 1969 to economists Ragnar Frisch and Jan Tinbergen

extra.why_interesting: Players assume all six prizes date from 1901; the economics prize is nearly seventy years younger and funded by a bank.
extra.verification_notes: The prize was established by Sveriges Riksbank in 1968 and first awarded in 1969, and it is not in Nobel's will.

explanation: The first five prizes started in 1901, but economics only arrived in 1969, funded by the Riksbank for its 300th anniversary.

question: In 2014, a 17-year-old from Pakistan became the youngest Nobel laureate in history. Who was she?
source_excerpt: The youngest Nobel Prize laureate ever, Malala Yousafzai, was only 17 years old at the time of the award.

extra.why_interesting: Nobel laureates are pictured as elderly professors; the youngest was a teenager still in school.
extra.verification_notes: Malala Yousafzai (b. 12 July 1997) won the 2014 Nobel Peace Prize at 17 and remains the youngest laureate; no newer record found (https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/peace/2014/yousafzai/speedread/).

explanation: Malala shared the Peace Prize with India's Kailash Satyarthi for her campaign for girls' education, two years after surviving a Taliban attack.

question: True or false: Dmitri Mendeleev, who created the periodic table of the elements, won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
source_excerpt: The academy ultimately chose Moissan by a single vote margin.

extra.why_interesting: The periodic table hangs in every chemistry classroom, so players assume its creator must have received chemistry's top honour.
extra.verification_notes: Mendeleev never won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry; the 1906 prize went to Henri Moissan by one vote over him (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dmitri_Mendeleev).

explanation: Mendeleev was nominated three times and lost the 1906 vote to Henri Moissan, then died in early 1907 before another chance came.

question: Her X-ray image known as Photo 51 helped reveal the double helix of DNA, but she died in 1958, four years before Watson, Crick and Wilkins collected their Nobel Prize. Who was she?
source_excerpt: Franklin died on 16 April 1958 at age 37 in Chelsea, London

extra.why_interesting: The DNA story is usually told as two men; the key image came from a woman who was gone before the prize was handed out.
extra.verification_notes: Franklin died 16 April 1958; Watson, Crick and Wilkins received the 1962 Nobel Prize; Photo 51 was made in her lab (taken by student Gosling), per Wikipedia.

explanation: Nobel rules forbid posthumous awards, so Franklin could never have been included when the 1962 Medicine prize was given.

question: Ernest Rutherford, famous for discovering the atomic nucleus, won his 1908 Nobel Prize in a category that surprised him so much he joked about it. Which category?
source_excerpt: Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1908 "for his investigations into the disintegration of the elements, and the chemistry of radioactive substances."

extra.why_interesting: The man who discovered the atomic nucleus is a physics icon, yet his Nobel came from a category he did not consider his own.
extra.verification_notes: Rutherford won the 1908 Nobel Prize in Chemistry (not Physics), and the well-known joke about his own 'transformation' from physicist to chemist fits the question.

explanation: The prize cited his work on the disintegration of elements, and Rutherford quipped that he had seen many transformations, but none as fast as his own from physicist to chemist.

question: Australian doctor Barry Marshall won the 2005 Nobel Prize in Medicine after deliberately drinking a broth of bacteria to prove they, not stress, cause which common condition?
source_excerpt: Marshall consumed a broth containing cultured H. pylori after undergoing a baseline endoscopy

extra.why_interesting: The condition was universally blamed on stress and spicy food; a scientist proved it was an infection by infecting himself.
extra.verification_notes: Marshall drank an H. pylori broth, and the work established the bacterium rather than stress as the cause of peptic (stomach) ulcers; the self-experiment itself produced gastritis, a minor nuance that doesn't undermine the answer (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barry_Marshall).

explanation: Marshall fell ill within days, confirming that Helicobacter pylori causes gastritis and ulcers, which are now cured with antibiotics instead of a lifetime of antacids.

question: Everyone remembers Ivan Pavlov for dogs drooling at a bell, but his 1904 Nobel Prize was for research on which bodily system?
source_excerpt: in recognition of his work on the physiology of digestion, through which knowledge on vital aspects of the subject has been transformed and enlarged

extra.why_interesting: Pavlov is a byword for conditioned reflexes, but the Nobel committee honoured him for something far less famous.
extra.verification_notes: Pavlov's 1904 Nobel was for his work on the physiology of digestion, which matches the claimed answer (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivan_Pavlov).

explanation: Pavlov won for mapping how the stomach and glands produce digestive juices; the salivating dogs started as a tool for that work and only later became his legacy.

question: Three of these scientists won two Nobel Prizes each. Which one won only once?
source_excerpt: Seven laureates have received more than one prize

extra.why_interesting: Bohr is the most famous name in the list, so players expect him to have the most honours; the two lesser-known men are the double winners.
extra.verification_notes: Curie, Bardeen and Sanger each won two Nobels; Bohr won only the 1922 Physics prize (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates).

explanation: Bardeen won Physics twice, for the transistor and for superconductivity, and Sanger won Chemistry twice for sequencing proteins and DNA, while Bohr took a single Physics prize in 1922.

question: In Venice, the famous Bridge of Sighs connects the Doge's Palace with what kind of building?
source_excerpt: The Bridge of Sighs connects the Doge's Palace with the New Prison across Rio di Palazzo in Venice.

extra.why_interesting: The name suggests lovers sighing on a gondola; the sighs were actually those of convicts getting their last look at Venice.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the bridge connects the Doge's Palace to the New Prison; nothing suggests this has changed (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bridge_of_Sighs).

explanation: Convicted prisoners crossed it from the courtrooms to the cells, supposedly sighing at their final glimpse of the lagoon through the stone grilles.

question: Its name means 'New Bridge', yet it is the oldest bridge still standing across the Seine in Paris. What is it called?
source_excerpt: The Pont Neuf ("New Bridge") is the oldest standing bridge across the river Seine in Paris, France.

extra.why_interesting: The name promises a new bridge; it is actually the oldest one in the city, four centuries old.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Pont Neuf ('New Bridge') is the oldest standing bridge across the Seine in Paris; no contradicting developments found.

explanation: Finished in 1607 under Henry IV, it was new compared with the medieval bridges of its day, and it has simply outlived all of them.

question: Which European capital only came into existence in 1873, when towns on opposite banks of the Danube were merged into one city?
source_excerpt: in 1873 Buda and Pest were officially merged with the third part, Óbuda (Old Buda), thus creating the new metropolis of Budapest.

extra.why_interesting: The city's name is a merger the player has said a thousand times without noticing it is two towns glued together.
extra.verification_notes: Budapest was formed on 17 Nov 1873 by merging Buda, Óbuda and Pest on opposite Danube banks; no newer event affects this (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Budapest).

explanation: Hilly Buda and Óbuda on the west bank joined flat Pest on the east bank, and the new city simply stitched the names together.

question: Which city has more bridges: Venice or Amsterdam?
source_excerpt: Amsterdam has more bridges than Venice, by a wide margin.

extra.why_interesting: Venice is the world's bridge city in everyone's head, but Amsterdam's canal grid needs more than three times as many crossings.
extra.verification_notes: Amsterdam has about 1,200–1,900 bridges against Venice's roughly 409, so the claimed answer holds under any counting method; sources are mostly tourism sites, and the Wikipedia article was not read directly.

explanation: Amsterdam's canal rings need roughly 1,500 bridges, while Venice gets by with around 400.

question: Which city in Bosnia and Herzegovina is famous for its 16th-century Ottoman stone bridge over the Neretva, destroyed in 1993 and rebuilt in 2004?
source_excerpt: The reconstructed bridge was inaugurated on 23 July 2004

extra.why_interesting: A 16th-century Ottoman stone arch survived four centuries only to fall in a 1990s war, then rose again as a UNESCO site.
extra.verification_notes: Stari Most in Mostar was built 1557–1566 over the Neretva, collapsed 9 Nov 1993 and was reopened 23 July 2004, per Wikipedia.

explanation: The city's very name comes from the bridge keepers, and the rebuilt Old Bridge is now a UNESCO World Heritage site where locals dive into the river for tourists.

question: The Øresund Bridge lets you drive or take a train from Copenhagen across the sea to which Swedish city?
source_excerpt: The bridge connects Copenhagen, Denmark and Malmö, Sweden... Four lanes of European route E20... Double-track Øresund Line

extra.why_interesting: A commute between two countries by road and rail across open sea, with the bridge dropping into a tunnel for the final stretch.
extra.verification_notes: The Øresund Bridge links Copenhagen with Malmö by road and rail, and I found no newer developments that change this (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%98resund_Bridge).

explanation: Opened in 2000, the link runs about 16 kilometres and halfway across it dives into a tunnel so ships can pass over the top.

question: The Millau Viaduct carries a motorway across a valley in southern France. Roughly how high does its tallest mast rise from the ground?
source_excerpt: 343 m (1,125 ft) (max pylon above ground)

extra.why_interesting: Nobody expects a motorway bridge in rural France to stand taller than the Eiffel Tower.
extra.verification_notes: Millau's tallest pylon reaches 343 m above ground, so 'About 350 metres' is the closest option; the question makes no 'tallest bridge' claim, so the later overtaking by Changtai doesn't affect it. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millau_Viaduct

explanation: At about 343 metres, its tallest mast overtops the Eiffel Tower, making it the tallest bridge structure in the world.

question: Which bridge over the Arno in Florence, famous for the jewellers' shops built along it, was the only bridge in the city spared when German troops retreated in 1944?
source_excerpt: the Ponte Vecchio was not destroyed by the German army during their retreat at the advance of the British 8th Army on 4 August 1944, unlike all the other bridges in Florence.

extra.why_interesting: Every other bridge in the city was blown up; the one lined with little goldsmiths' shops was spared, reportedly on direct orders.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the Ponte Vecchio was the only Florence bridge not destroyed by retreating German forces in August 1944; no newer developments affect this.

explanation: Every other Florentine bridge was blown up to slow the Allies, but the medieval shop-lined bridge was left standing, reportedly on Hitler's express order.

question: Dublin's cast-iron footbridge over the Liffey, opened in 1816, takes its popular name from the small toll once charged to cross it. What is the bridge called?
source_excerpt: Official Name: Liffey Bridge (though commonly called Ha'penny Bridge)

extra.why_interesting: A grand-sounding landmark turns out to be named after the smallest coin in the purse.
extra.verification_notes: Ha'penny Bridge opened in 1816 and is named for the ha'penny toll; its official name, Liffey Bridge, isn't what the question asks for.

explanation: Pedestrians paid half a penny to cross for about a century, and although the toll vanished in 1919 the nickname never did.

question: Which European capital is the only national capital in the world whose city limits border two other countries?
source_excerpt: the only national capital to have land borders with two other sovereign states

extra.why_interesting: The player expects a capital to sit safely in the middle of its country; this one is wedged into a corner touching two neighbours at once.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Bratislava is the only national capital with land borders with two other sovereign states (Austria and Hungary); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bratislava

explanation: The Slovak capital sits in the far south-west corner of its country, touching both Austria and Hungary, with Vienna barely an hour away.

question: True or false: the Thames is the longest river in the United Kingdom.
source_excerpt: The River Severn is the longest river in Great Britain, with a length of 220 miles (354 km).

extra.why_interesting: The Thames is the river everyone can name, so the player assumes it must also be the longest; a quieter river on the Welsh border beats it by a few kilometres.
extra.verification_notes: The Severn (354 km) is the longest river in Great Britain and the UK, longer than the Thames (~346 km), so 'False' is correct.

explanation: The Severn, rising in Wales and reaching the sea near Bristol, is slightly longer at roughly 354 kilometres against the Thames at about 346.

question: Which European capital stands on the banks of the Vltava, the river made famous by Smetana's symphonic poem?
source_excerpt: The river flows north across Bohemia, through Český Krumlov, České Budějovice and Prague.

extra.why_interesting: A straightforward anchor fact, and a chance for a quick win for players who know Smetana's famous musical portrait of the river.
extra.verification_notes: The Vltava flows through Prague, the Czech capital, and Smetana's symphonic poem Vltava depicts it; no newer development changes this (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vltava).

explanation: The Vltava, known in German as the Moldau, flows under Prague's Charles Bridge before joining the Elbe further north.

question: In which Italian city did a Medici grand duke evict the butchers from the shops on the famous old bridge and hand them to goldsmiths, who are still there today?
source_excerpt: a decree was made in 1565 that excluded butchers from this bridge (only goldsmiths and jewellers are allowed) that is in effect to this day.

extra.why_interesting: Everyone knows the glittering jewellers on the bridge; the surprise is that the Medici installed them to replace butchers, because the smell of offal drifting up to the duke's private corridor above the shops was unbearable.
extra.verification_notes: Ponte Vecchio in Florence had its butchers expelled by a Medici grand duke (Cosimo I per Wikipedia, Ferdinando I in 1593 per other sources), and goldsmiths and jewellers remain; the question's unnamed 'a Medici grand duke' covers both.

explanation: That is the Ponte Vecchio over the Arno: Ferdinando I banished the butchers in 1593, reportedly because the stench reached the Vasari Corridor running above the shops.

question: Venice and Amsterdam are famous for their bridges, but one German port city has more bridges than both of them combined. Which city is it?
alternative_answers: Free and Hanseatic City of Hamburg
topic: Rivers, bridges and famous cities of Europe
source_excerpt: a total number of 2,496 bridges in Hamburg, many more than cities like Venice, Amsterdam or Saint Petersburg.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume the European bridge capital must be Venice or Amsterdam, the cities famous for canals. The real record-holder is a German port most people never associate with water at all, and it beats both canal cities put together.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia's list of bridges in Hamburg cites 2,496 bridges, well above Amsterdam (~1,200) plus Venice (~400) combined; no newer development contradicts this.

explanation: Hamburg sits on the Elbe, the Alster and a web of canals, and counts around 2,500 bridges inside its city limits, far more than Venice's roughly 400 and Amsterdam's roughly 1,500 together.

question: Which island nation dropped the name Ceylon in 1972?
source_excerpt: Later, on 7 September 1978, it was changed to the Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka.

extra.why_interesting: The old name survives on tea packets everywhere, so players feel the click of connecting the two.
extra.verification_notes: Ceylon became the Republic of Sri Lanka in 1972; the 1978 renaming to Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka doesn't change this.

explanation: Ceylon lives on only as a brand of tea; the country itself has been Sri Lanka since 1972.

question: Which Asian country is the only one in the world whose national flag is not a rectangle?
source_excerpt: It is the only non-rectangular national flag in the world and the only one that is taller than it is wide.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume every flag is a rectangle; the one exception is a Himalayan country most people can picture once prompted.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Nepal's flag is the only non-rectangular national flag in the world; no recent change found.

explanation: Nepal's flag is two stacked triangles, carrying a moon and a sun, and it is the only non-rectangular national flag on Earth.

question: The Mughal emperor Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal in Agra in memory of whom?
source_excerpt: It was commissioned in 1631 by the fifth Mughal emperor, Shah Jahan (r. 1628–1658), to house the tomb of his late wife, Mumtaz Mahal

extra.why_interesting: The most photographed palace-looking building in Asia is actually a tomb built out of grief.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the Taj Mahal was commissioned by Shah Jahan to house the tomb of his wife Mumtaz Mahal (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taj_Mahal).

explanation: It is not a palace but a mausoleum, raised after Mumtaz Mahal died in childbirth in 1631.

question: Roughly how many islands make up the Philippines?
source_excerpt: The Philippines is an archipelago that comprises 7,641 islands

extra.why_interesting: Most players picture a handful of big islands; the true count is in the thousands, and the buckets let them reason their way there.
extra.verification_notes: The Philippines has 7,641 islands, which falls in the 'Thousands' option; the older 7,107 figure gives the same answer (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_the_Philippines).

explanation: The official count is a little over 7,600 islands, though only around 2,000 of them are inhabited.

question: Which country is the largest in the world with no coastline on an ocean?
source_excerpt: Kazakhstan is the world's largest landlocked country by area, with 2,724,900 km².

extra.why_interesting: Players reach for Mongolia; the real answer is a country larger than all of Western Europe that rarely gets a second thought.
extra.verification_notes: Kazakhstan is the largest landlocked country by area; its only coast is on the Caspian, an inland sea, so 'no ocean coastline' is accurate (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landlocked_country).

explanation: Kazakhstan covers about 2.7 million square kilometres, roughly five times the size of France, and touches only the inland Caspian Sea.

question: Which is the only country in Southeast Asia with no sea coast at all?
source_excerpt: Laos...is a country in Mainland Southeast Asia, and the only landlocked country in Southeast Asia.

extra.why_interesting: Southeast Asia is all peninsulas and archipelagos, so a player can mentally walk the map and eliminate until one country is left.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Laos is the only landlocked country in Southeast Asia; no newer developments found that change this.

explanation: Laos is wedged between Thailand, Vietnam, Cambodia, Myanmar and China, with the Mekong River as its main highway instead of a port.

question: Borobudur, the largest Buddhist temple in the world, stands in which Muslim-majority country?
source_excerpt: recorded in the Guinness Book of World Records as the world's largest Buddhist temple

extra.why_interesting: The biggest Buddhist monument on Earth stands in the country with the world's largest Muslim population, which flips the player's expectation.
extra.verification_notes: Borobudur is in Central Java, Indonesia (Muslim-majority) and is recognised by Guinness as the world's largest Buddhist temple; no newer event found that overturns this.

explanation: The ninth-century temple on Java was built centuries before Islam arrived, and Indonesia now has more Muslims than any other country.

question: The world's tallest indoor waterfall, about 40 metres high, pours through the middle of which airport?
source_excerpt: The Rain Vortex is the world's largest and tallest indoor waterfall, standing at 40 metres (130 ft) high.

extra.why_interesting: A waterfall inside an airport sounds like fiction; the answer rewards anyone who has flown through Asia's showpiece hub.
extra.verification_notes: Rain Vortex at Jewel Changi Airport is 40 m and still recognised as the world's tallest indoor waterfall; no newer record-holder found.

explanation: The Rain Vortex at Changi's Jewel complex drops seven storeys through a glass dome, surrounded by an indoor forest.

question: The world's highest mountain carries the surname of a British surveyor. What do the Nepalese call it?
source_excerpt: The Nepali designation is Sagarmāthā (सगरमाथा)

extra.why_interesting: Everyone knows the mountain, almost nobody knows that its global name is a surveyor's surname and that locals call it something else entirely.
extra.verification_notes: Everest is named after British surveyor Sir George Everest and is called Sagarmatha in Nepal, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Everest.

explanation: Sagarmatha means roughly 'forehead of the sky' in Nepali, while Tibetans across the border call the same peak Chomolungma.

question: Which Himalayan kingdom famously measures its national progress with an index of Gross National Happiness?
source_excerpt: invented by the 4th King of Bhutan, Jigme Singye Wangchuck

extra.why_interesting: Players assume every government chases GDP; one small kingdom publicly decided wellbeing is the headline statistic instead.
extra.verification_notes: Bhutan originated and uses Gross National Happiness, and it remains a Himalayan kingdom (constitutional monarchy), per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gross_National_Happiness

explanation: Bhutan's fourth king declared in the 1970s that Gross National Happiness matters more than Gross National Product, and the idea is now written into the country's constitution.

question: Indonesia is the world's largest island nation. Roughly how many islands does it have?
source_excerpt: According to the Law No. 9/1996 on Maritime Territory of Indonesia, there are 17,508 officially listed islands.

extra.why_interesting: Most people picture Indonesia as Java, Bali, Sumatra and a handful of others; learning that the count runs into the tens of thousands, most of them uninhabited, reframes the whole country as a scattered ocean nation.
extra.verification_notes: All credible counts (13,466 to 18,307; official ~17,000) fall in the tens of thousands range per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_islands_of_Indonesia.

explanation: Indonesia counts around seventeen thousand islands, most of them uninhabited, stretched across a distance wider than the continental United States.

question: Which Tokyo railway station holds the Guinness World Record as the busiest station on Earth, serving more than three million passengers every day?
source_excerpt: The station was used by an average of 3.59 million people per day in 2018, making it the world's busiest railway station by far (and registered as such with Guinness World Records).

extra.why_interesting: Players expect the world's busiest station to be a grand central terminus like Tokyo Station or a Paris or London hub; instead it is a commuter interchange in a Tokyo business district that most tourists only know as a neighbourhood name.
extra.verification_notes: Guinness World Records recognises Shinjuku as the busiest station; Wikipedia gives 3.59M daily users in 2018, though Guinness's 2022 figure is 2.7M (pandemic dip), a minor wrinkle.

explanation: Shinjuku Station handles over three and a half million passengers a day through more than two hundred exits, and it is a commuter interchange rather than the city's main terminus.

question: Lemurs live in the wild on only one island nation on Earth. Which one?
source_excerpt: They are endemic to the island of Madagascar.

extra.why_interesting: Players know lemurs are African primates but may not realise the entire group is confined to a single island, a result of tens of millions of years of isolation.
extra.verification_notes: Lemurs are endemic to Madagascar per Wikipedia; any Comoros/Mayotte populations are introduced, so the answer stands.

explanation: Lemurs evolved in isolation after their ancestors reached the island tens of millions of years ago, and more than a hundred species live nowhere else.

question: Mount Kilimanjaro, the highest mountain in Africa, stands in which country?
source_excerpt: the highest mountain in Africa and the highest free-standing mountain above sea level in the world, at 5,895 m (19,341 ft)

extra.why_interesting: Many people picture Kilimanjaro from the Kenyan side, where it famously looms behind Amboseli's elephants, and assume it belongs to Kenya.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Kilimanjaro is in Tanzania and is Africa's highest mountain; no newer developments contradict this.

explanation: The classic postcard view of elephants beneath the snowy summit is shot from Kenya, but the mountain itself lies just across the border in Tanzania.

question: Which African country has three capital cities, each hosting a different branch of its government?
source_excerpt: South Africa has no legally defined capital city, with the country's three branches of government split over different cities: Pretoria (executive), Bloemfontein (judicial) and Cape Town (legislative).

extra.why_interesting: Players assume every country has one capital; the three-way split dates from the 1910 compromise that unified the old colonies.
extra.verification_notes: South Africa's three capitals (Pretoria executive, Cape Town legislative, Bloemfontein judicial) are confirmed, and no African country has three such capitals and no 2026 change affects it.

explanation: Pretoria holds the executive, Cape Town the parliament and Bloemfontein the top courts, a compromise struck when the country was unified in 1910.

question: Since South Sudan broke away in 2011, which country has been the largest in Africa by area?
source_excerpt: Algeria has been the largest country in Africa and the Arab world since the division of the Sudan in 2011.

extra.why_interesting: Older atlases and school memories say Sudan; the 2011 split quietly handed the title to a North African country most players would not pick first.
extra.verification_notes: Algeria has been Africa's largest country by area since South Sudan's 2011 secession, per Wikipedia's list of African countries by area (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_African_countries_by_area); no newer change found.

explanation: Sudan lost about a quarter of its territory in the split, and Algeria, with more than 2.3 million square kilometres of mostly Sahara, moved to the top.

question: Monrovia, the capital of Liberia, is named after which American president?
source_excerpt: Monrovia is named in honor of U.S. President James Monroe, a prominent supporter of the colonization of Liberia and the American Colonization Society (ACS).

extra.why_interesting: The name hides in plain sight: once the player hears 'Monrovia' and thinks of US presidents, the answer clicks, and the back-story of Liberia's founding is the payoff.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Monrovia is named for President James Monroe, and it remains Liberia's capital.

explanation: Liberia was founded in the 1820s as a settlement for freed American slaves, and the capital honoured Monroe, the president who backed the project.

question: Ethiopia's official calendar is unusual: how many months does it have?
source_excerpt: The Ethiopian calendar has twelve months, all thirty days long, and five or six epagomenal days, which form a thirteenth month.

extra.why_interesting: Everyone assumes twelve months is universal; Ethiopia's tourism slogan '13 months of sunshine' is the fun confirmation.
extra.verification_notes: The Ethiopian calendar is widely described as having 13 months (12 of 30 days plus Pagume of 5-6 days); no reform was found in the Wikipedia article, and I did not search separately for recent news.

explanation: Twelve months of exactly 30 days are followed by a tiny thirteenth month of five or six days, and the whole calendar runs about seven years behind the Western one.

question: Which scaly, ant-eating mammal found in Africa and Asia is widely reported as the most trafficked mammal in the world?
source_excerpt: This makes them the most trafficked animal in the world.

extra.why_interesting: Players expect elephants or rhinos; the real answer is a shy, scaly anteater-like creature most people have never seen.
extra.verification_notes: Pangolins are widely described as the most trafficked mammal; they are scaly, ant-eating, and found in Africa and Asia, and 2026 sources still say so.

explanation: Its keratin scales are prized in traditional medicine, and it is the only mammal fully covered in scales, rolling into a ball when threatened.

question: Three of these countries were once Portuguese colonies. Which one was not?
source_excerpt: continued to Cape Cross, in present-day Namibia, near the Tropic of Capricorn

extra.why_interesting: All four are southern or western African states that gained independence in the same late-colonial era, so only colonial history separates them.
extra.verification_notes: Namibia was German then South African-ruled, never a Portuguese colony; Angola, Mozambique and Guinea-Bissau were Portuguese colonies (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_Empire).

explanation: Namibia was German South West Africa until the First World War and then run by South Africa until 1990, while the other three were Portuguese until 1974 and 1975.

question: A furry, guinea-pig-sized animal that suns itself on African rocks is one of the elephant's closest living relatives. What is it?
source_excerpt: are much more closely related to elephants and sirenians

extra.why_interesting: A guinea-pig-sized animal being kin to the largest land mammal defies every intuition about what relatives should look like.
extra.verification_notes: Hyraxes bask on rocks and are, with sirenians, the elephant's closest living relatives (Paenungulata); 'one of' covers the manatee overlap and the furry rock-basking clue is unique to hyraxes.

explanation: Hyraxes and elephants share a common ancestor from tens of millions of years ago, and hyraxes even have tiny tusk-like incisors to prove it.

question: In 1896, Emperor Menelik II of Ethiopia crushed an invading European army at the Battle of Adwa. Which European country was defeated?
source_excerpt: Ethiopian Empire against the Kingdom of Italy; 1 March 1896; Ethiopian victory

extra.why_interesting: Players know Ethiopia was never colonised but rarely know it was won on a battlefield; the later 1930s Italian invasion under Mussolini is a foothold for reasoning.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Ethiopia under Menelik II defeated the Kingdom of Italy at Adwa on 1 March 1896.

explanation: It was the first decisive defeat of a European colonial army by an African state, and Italy only returned for revenge under Mussolini in 1935.

question: The capital city of which African country, founded as a settlement for freed American slaves, is named after a President of the United States?
source_excerpt: Monrovia is named in honor of U.S. President James Monroe, a prominent supporter of the colonization of Liberia.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume African capitals carry African or European colonial names; discovering one honours an American president is a surprise, and the clue 'freed slaves from America' gives a reasoning path to Liberia even for those who never knew Monrovia's origin.
extra.verification_notes: Monrovia, capital of Liberia, is named for President James Monroe and was founded as a settlement for free people of color from the US; no change of capital found (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monrovia).

explanation: Monrovia honours James Monroe, the fifth US president, who backed the 1820s project that sent freed African Americans to settle the West African coast.

question: Which South American country still keeps a navy, complete with admirals, even though it lost its entire coastline to Chile in the 1880s?
topic: The Americas: countries, history and landmarks
source_excerpt: Chile defeated Peru and Bolivia, and conquered the Litoral Department which included all of the Bolivian coastline.

extra.why_interesting: A player assumes a navy needs a sea; the answer is a landlocked country that keeps admirals and sailors on a mountain lake while waiting to get its coast back.
extra.verification_notes: Bolivia lost its coast to Chile in the War of the Pacific and still maintains a navy with admirals; no disbandment found (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivian_Naval_Force).

explanation: Bolivia has been landlocked since the War of the Pacific, but its navy trains on Lake Titicaca and the country still formally claims a route back to the sea.

question: Which capital city, built by the Spanish on the bed of a drained lake, is sinking so fast that some of its old churches now lean?
topic: The Americas: countries, history and landmarks
source_excerpt: the city has sunk as much as nine meters (30 feet) in some areas, and it continues to sink almost 50 centimetres (20 in) every year.

extra.why_interesting: A player pictures a capital on solid ground; this one sits on a former lake and is visibly dropping, tilting churches and cracking pipes.
extra.verification_notes: Mexico City was built on drained Lake Texcoco and is sinking, with colonial churches such as the Metropolitan Cathedral tilting; no newer events contradict this.

explanation: The Aztecs built Tenochtitlan on an island in Lake Texcoco, and the modern city on the drained lakebed sinks as water is pumped from the soft clay beneath it.

question: Brazil shares a land border with every other country in South America except two. Which two?
topic: The Americas: countries, history and landmarks
source_excerpt: Brazil has borders with every country in South America with the exception of Chile and Ecuador, totalling 16,885 kilometres (10,492 mi).

extra.why_interesting: The player must mentally walk Brazil's enormous frontier and realise the two gaps are both on the far Pacific side, hidden behind the Andes.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Brazil borders all South American countries except Chile and Ecuador; no newer developments affect this.

explanation: Both sit on the Pacific side of the Andes, with Peru and Bolivia filling the gap between them and Brazil.

question: Which South American country has Dutch as its official language?
topic: The Americas: countries, history and landmarks
source_excerpt: Suriname is the only independent state outside Europe where Dutch is the official and prevailing language of government, business, media, and education.

extra.why_interesting: A player expects a continent of Spanish and Portuguese; a small corner of the Atlantic coast still runs its parliament and schools in Dutch.
extra.verification_notes: Dutch is Suriname's official language and no other South American country has it as an official language; no recent change found (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suriname).

explanation: The Netherlands ruled it as Dutch Guiana until 1975, and today Suriname's Dutch speakers sit next to English-speaking Guyana and French-run French Guiana.

question: The United States still sends Cuba an annual rent payment for the Guantánamo Bay naval base. Roughly how much is it?
topic: The Americas: countries, history and landmarks
source_excerpt: Subsequent adjustments occurred in 1973 ($3,676.50) and 1974 ($4,085).

extra.why_interesting: A player imagines a superpower paying serious money for a strategic base; the real figure is a token sum fixed over a century ago, and Cuba won't even bank it.
extra.verification_notes: The annual rent is $4,085, matching 'around 4,000 dollars', and nothing found shows it has changed; see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guantanamo_Bay_Naval_Base

explanation: The 1903 lease set the rent at 2,000 dollars in gold coin, now reckoned at about 4,000 dollars, and Cuba has pointedly left the cheques uncashed since Castro took power.

question: Easter Island, with its giant stone heads, sits in the Pacific more than 3,000 kilometres from the mainland. Which country does it belong to?
topic: The Americas: countries, history and landmarks
source_excerpt: an island and special territory of Chile in the southeastern Pacific Ocean

extra.why_interesting: The island feels like a Polynesian world apart; the surprise is that it belongs to a South American country thousands of kilometres away.
extra.verification_notes: Easter Island is a special territory of Chile, about 3,512 km from the Chilean mainland, per Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Easter_Island); no sovereignty change found.

explanation: Chile annexed the island in 1888, and today the moai are among the most remote inhabited landmarks on Earth, roughly 3,500 kilometres west of the Chilean coast.

question: After the United States, which was the second country in the Americas to win its independence, in 1804, after a slave uprising defeated Napoleon's troops?
topic: The Americas: countries, history and landmarks
source_excerpt: Haiti declared independence on January 1, 1804, making it the second independent nation in the Americas after the United States.

extra.why_interesting: Players reach for Mexico or Argentina; the real second was a small Caribbean nation that beat Napoleon's army, decades before the Spanish colonies broke free.
extra.verification_notes: Haiti declared independence on 1 Jan 1804 after defeating Napoleon's forces, making it the second independent nation in the Americas after the US (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haitian_Revolution).

explanation: Haiti's revolution was the only slave revolt in history to found a nation, and it came almost two decades before most of Spanish America broke away.

question: Canada's rival cities could not agree on a capital, so in 1857 the choice was handed to a monarch in London. Who picked Ottawa?
topic: The Americas: countries, history and landmarks
source_excerpt: The Queen sent a letter to colonial authorities selecting Ottawa as the capital, effective 31 December 1857.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume capitals are chosen by the country itself; Canada's was personally picked by a monarch an ocean away, over all its big cities.
extra.verification_notes: Queen Victoria selected Ottawa as capital of the Province of Canada in December 1857, on the Governor General's advice; no later events change this.

explanation: Victoria chose the small lumber town partly because it sat safely back from the US border and on the line between English and French Canada.

question: The great pyramid at Chichén Itzá in Mexico has 91 steps on each of its four sides. Add the single platform on top, and the total matches what?
topic: The Americas: countries, history and landmarks
source_excerpt: each of the four sides has approximately 91 steps which, when combined with the temple platform as the final step, totals 365 steps

extra.why_interesting: The stem hands the player the arithmetic (91 times 4 plus 1) and lets them discover the Maya calendar hidden in the stone themselves.
extra.verification_notes: El Castillo's 4×91 steps plus the top platform equals 365, the days in the Haabʼ solar year; no newer developments contradict it (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Castillo,_Chichen_Itza).

explanation: Four sides of 91 steps make 364, and the summit platform brings it to 365, a solar calendar built into a Maya temple.

question: The classic straw Panama hat has traditionally been woven in which country?
topic: The Americas: countries, history and landmarks
source_excerpt: Although commonly called 'Panama hat' in English, the hat has its origin in Ecuador.

extra.why_interesting: The name points the player straight at the wrong country; the hats come from the neighbour further south and only passed through Panama on their way to the world.
extra.verification_notes: Panama hats are traditionally woven in Ecuador (toquilla straw), recognised by UNESCO in 2012; see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panama_hat

explanation: Ecuadorian weavers in Montecristi and Cuenca made them for centuries, but the hats reached the world through the port of Panama, and the name stuck.

question: In 1867 the United States bought Alaska for about 7 million dollars, a deal critics called a folly. Which country sold it?
topic: The Americas: countries, history and landmarks
source_excerpt: Seller: The Russian Empire; Price: $7.2 million; opponents labeled the acquisition 'Seward's Folly'.

extra.why_interesting: Players know the US bought Alaska but often forget from whom; the seller, a nation now on the far side of the Bering Strait, makes the geography click.
extra.verification_notes: Russia (the Russian Empire) sold Alaska to the US in 1867 for $7.2 million, and critics did call it 'Seward's Folly' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alaska_Purchase).

explanation: The Russian Empire sold its distant, loss-making colony for roughly 2 cents a hectare, three decades before the Klondike gold rush made the purchase look brilliant.

question: Which South American country is the only one with a coastline on both the Pacific Ocean and the Caribbean Sea?
topic: The Americas: countries, history and landmarks
source_excerpt: the Caribbean Sea to the north ... the Pacific Ocean to the west

extra.why_interesting: Players picture the continent as having an Atlantic side and a Pacific side and assume several countries straddle both; in fact only one does, and it sits right at the top where the continent narrows toward Panama.
extra.verification_notes: Colombia borders both the Caribbean Sea and the Pacific Ocean, and no other South American country does; Panama is in North America.

explanation: Colombia sits at the continent's northwest corner, with Cartagena on the Caribbean and Buenaventura on the Pacific. Every other South American country touches at most one ocean.

question: In 2011, Samoa went to bed on the 29th of December and woke up on the 31st, deleting a whole day to be closer in time to Australia and New Zealand. What did the country move across to make that happen?
source_excerpt: In 2011, Samoa shifted back to the west side of the IDL by removing Friday, 30 December 2011 from its calendar.

extra.why_interesting: A whole country deleting a calendar day sounds impossible; the answer is a line on the map that governments can simply decide to be on the other side of.
extra.verification_notes: Samoa skipped 30 Dec 2011 by crossing to the west side of the International Date Line to align with Australia/NZ; no later change reported (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Date_Line).

explanation: Samoa jumped from being among the last places on Earth to end the day to among the first to start it, so Friday the 30th of December 2011 simply never happened there.

question: Web addresses ending in .tv are popular with streaming and video sites, but the ending is actually the country code of which small Pacific island nation?
source_excerpt: GoDaddy signed a contract with the government of Tuvalu to manage .tv registrations, increasing yearly payments to the government of Tuvalu to $10 million.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume .tv stands for television; it is actually a country code, and that country is one of the smallest on Earth.
extra.verification_notes: The .tv country code top-level domain is assigned to Tuvalu and is still active, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/.tv; no newer event contradicts this.

explanation: Tuvalu has only around eleven thousand people, and leasing its lucky two-letter domain has for years brought in a notable share of the government's income.

question: Mainland Australia's highest mountain, at about 2,228 metres, is named after a national hero of which European country?
source_excerpt: named by the Polish explorer Paweł (Paul) Edmund Strzelecki in 1840, in honour of Tadeusz Kościuszko

extra.why_interesting: Players expect an English or Aboriginal name for Australia's highest peak; instead it honours a Polish freedom fighter who never set foot in Australia.
extra.verification_notes: Mount Kosciuszko (2,228 m) was named by Strzelecki for Tadeusz Kościuszko, a Polish national hero; no newer events found that change this.

explanation: Polish explorer Paweł Strzelecki climbed it in 1840 and named it after Tadeusz Kościuszko, the general who fought for both Polish and American independence.

question: Australia maintains a fence over 5,000 kilometres long, one of the longest structures ever built, to keep which animal away from its sheep?
source_excerpt: The Dingo Fence is 5,614 kilometres (3,488 mi) long

extra.why_interesting: A fence longer than the distance from Lisbon to Moscow sounds like a border wall; the surprise is it was built against a wild dog.
extra.verification_notes: The Dingo Fence is 5,614 km long and was built to keep dingoes/wild dogs from sheep; recent extensions only add length (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dingo_Fence).

explanation: The fence runs from Queensland to South Australia and is longer than the distance from Lisbon to Moscow.

question: In which year did the Australian military send soldiers armed with machine guns to fight a population of emus in Western Australia, in a campaign the birds famously won?
source_excerpt: Second attempt: November 13 - December 10, 1932; Royal Australian Artillery's 7th Heavy Artillery with two Lewis guns.

extra.why_interesting: Players picture a colonial-era or Victorian absurdity; the surprise is that it happened in the age of machine guns and radio, between the world wars.
extra.verification_notes: The Emu War occurred in Nov–Dec 1932 in Western Australia, with Lewis guns used by the Royal Australian Artillery; later requests for military help were refused, so nothing supersedes it.

explanation: The so-called Great Emu War ran for a few weeks late in 1932, and the fast-moving birds proved so hard to hit that the troops withdrew.

question: Modern bungee jumping was inspired by a ritual on Pentecost Island, where men leap from tall wooden towers with only vines tied to their ankles. Pentecost belongs to which Pacific country?
source_excerpt: men in the southern part of the island jump from tall towers (around 20 to 30 metres, 70 to 100 ft) with vines tied to their feet

extra.why_interesting: Players think bungee jumping was invented by thrill-seekers in New Zealand; its origin is a centuries-old ritual on a Pacific island most have never heard of.
extra.verification_notes: Pentecost Island is part of Vanuatu and its Gol land-diving ritual is the recognised inspiration for bungee jumping (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pentecost_Island).

explanation: The land diving ritual is tied to the yam harvest, and British thrill-seekers who saw it in the 1970s went on to stage the first bungee jumps with elastic cords.

question: At the Rio 2016 Olympics, which Pacific island nation won its first ever Olympic medal, and it was a gold, in the new sport of rugby sevens?
source_excerpt: Fiji earned its first ever Olympic medal at these Games, with a gold from the men's rugby sevens team (led by Kolinisau).

extra.why_interesting: Players assume a nation's first Olympic medal is usually a modest bronze; this one went straight to gold and triggered a national holiday.
extra.verification_notes: Fiji won its first-ever Olympic medal, gold in men's rugby sevens at Rio 2016, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiji_at_the_2016_Summer_Olympics.

explanation: Fiji thrashed Great Britain in the final, the government declared a public holiday, and the coach's face later appeared on a seven-dollar banknote.

question: Which Australian mammal lays eggs, has a bill like a duck, and in the male carries venom in a spur on its hind legs?
source_excerpt: The spurs of the male inject venom, which is powerful enough to inflict pain in humans.

extra.why_interesting: Players know the bill and the egg-laying as a curiosity; the venom is the detail that makes them realise how strange the animal really is.
extra.verification_notes: Platypus is an egg-laying Australian mammal with a duck-like bill, and males have venomous hind-leg spurs, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platypus.

explanation: When British scientists first saw a preserved specimen in 1799, some suspected it was a hoax stitched together from different animals.

question: In the film 2001: A Space Odyssey, what is the name of the spaceship's computer that turns against the crew?
topic: Robots, AI and the future of technology
source_excerpt: Faced with the prospect of disconnection, HAL attempts to kill the astronauts in order to protect and continue the mission.

extra.why_interesting: A warm-up everyone has a path to: the calm red eye that says 'I'm sorry, Dave' is the archetype of the rogue AI, and the IBM-letters coincidence is a fun payoff.
extra.verification_notes: HAL 9000 is the Discovery One computer that turns on the crew in 2001: A Space Odyssey; nothing found that changes this (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HAL_9000).

explanation: Each letter of HAL sits one step before I, B and M in the alphabet, but author Arthur C. Clarke always insisted that was pure coincidence.

question: In 2011, an IBM computer called Watson beat two human champions on which American TV quiz show?
topic: Robots, AI and the future of technology
source_excerpt: in 2011, the Watson computer system competed on Jeopardy! against champions Brad Rutter and Ken Jennings, winning the first-place prize of US$1 million.

extra.why_interesting: Players remember a computer beating humans at something, and the twist is that it was a word-heavy quiz show rather than chess.
extra.verification_notes: Watson won on Jeopardy! in 2011 against Brad Rutter and Ken Jennings; a fixed historical event that nothing later has overtaken.

explanation: Beaten champion Ken Jennings scribbled under his final answer: I, for one, welcome our new computer overlords.

question: In 2017, a humanoid robot named Sophia became the first robot ever granted citizenship of a country. Which country?
topic: Robots, AI and the future of technology
source_excerpt: the first robot to receive legal personhood in any country

extra.why_interesting: Players expect a tech-forward country like Japan or Estonia; the actual answer is a surprise and still checkable in every major outlet.
extra.verification_notes: Saudi Arabia granted Sophia citizenship on 25 Oct 2017, the first robot to receive legal personhood in any country, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sophia_(robot).

explanation: The announcement came at an investment conference in Riyadh, and Sophia herself was built by Hanson Robotics in Hong Kong.

question: ELIZA, a 1966 computer program that was one of the first to hold a typed conversation, imitated which profession?
topic: Robots, AI and the future of technology
source_excerpt: simulated a psychotherapist of the Rogerian school (in which the therapist often reflects back the patient's words to the patient)

extra.why_interesting: A chatbot from the 1960s already fooled people emotionally, and the profession it mimicked is the one where reflecting questions back is a legitimate technique.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms ELIZA's DOCTOR script simulated a Rogerian psychotherapist, released 1966, among the first chatbots.

explanation: It mostly turned your own statements back into questions, yet its creator Joseph Weizenbaum was alarmed by how emotionally attached people became to it.

question: In his famous 1950 paper, Alan Turing never used the phrase 'Turing test'. What name did he give his test for machine intelligence?
topic: Robots, AI and the future of technology
source_excerpt: The test was introduced as the imitation game by Turing in his 1950 paper 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence.'

extra.why_interesting: Players know the Turing test and probably know the Cumberbatch film title, but few have connected the two.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Turing called it the 'imitation game' in his 1950 paper and did not use the phrase 'Turing test'.

explanation: That phrase later became the title of the 2014 film about Turing starring Benedict Cumberbatch.

question: Geoffrey Hinton, often called the godfather of AI, won a Nobel Prize in 2024 for his work on neural networks. In which Nobel category?
topic: Robots, AI and the future of technology
source_excerpt: for foundational discoveries and inventions that enable machine learning with artificial neural networks.

extra.why_interesting: There is no Nobel for computing, so the player must work out which existing prize a computer scientist could possibly win, and physics is a real surprise.
extra.verification_notes: Hinton shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics with John Hopfield, per Wikipedia; the Nobel site itself was inaccessible (403).

explanation: There is no Nobel for computer science, so the committee honoured him and John Hopfield in physics, while the same year's chemistry prize went to DeepMind's AlphaFold creators.

question: ChatGPT launched in November 2022. Roughly how long did it take to reach an estimated 100 million users?
topic: Robots, AI and the future of technology
source_excerpt: ChatGPT gained one million users in five days and 100 million in two months.

extra.why_interesting: Everyone remembers it appearing fast, but the actual figure of two months, versus years for Instagram, is still startling.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia and the UBS/Similarweb analysis both put ChatGPT at about 100 million users roughly two months after its November 2022 launch (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ChatGPT).

explanation: Analysts at UBS put it at 100 million monthly users by January 2023, the fastest consumer app growth ever recorded at the time, compared with about nine months for TikTok and more than two years for Instagram.

question: In 2004, the US military research agency DARPA offered one million dollars to the first self-driving car to finish a roughly 230-kilometre desert course. How many of the 15 finalists completed it?
topic: Robots, AI and the future of technology
source_excerpt: None of the robot vehicles finished the route.

extra.why_interesting: Players guess a small number of finishers; the real answer is zero, which shows how far self-driving cars have come in two decades.
extra.verification_notes: None of the 15 finalists finished the 2004 DARPA Grand Challenge, and the $1M prize went unclaimed; the 230 km course length is approximately right (sources vary between about 228 and 241 km).

explanation: The best vehicle, Carnegie Mellon's Sandstorm, got stuck after about 12 kilometres, yet just one year later five cars finished and Stanford's Stanley took the prize.

question: NASA's Opportunity rover landed on Mars in January 2004. Roughly how long did it keep working?
topic: Robots, AI and the future of technology
source_excerpt: Opportunity was operational on Mars for 5111 sols (14 years, 138 days on Earth).

extra.why_interesting: Players assume a Mars robot wears out in a year or two; the truth is a machine built for three months running for nearly fifteen years.
extra.verification_notes: Opportunity operated on Mars from January 2004 until contact was lost in June 2018, about 14 years, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opportunity_(rover).

explanation: It was designed for just 90 days, but kept driving and sending data until a planet-wide dust storm silenced it in 2018, more than fourteen years later.

question: The first industrial robot, called Unimate, began work on a car factory production line. In which year?
topic: Robots, AI and the future of technology
source_excerpt: Unimate was the first industrial robot, which worked on a General Motors assembly line at the Inland Fisher Guide Plant in Ewing Township, New Jersey, in 1961.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume factory robots arrived with the microchip era in the 1970s or 80s, but the first one clocked in before the Beatles' first record.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Unimate, the first industrial robot, worked on a GM assembly line in Ewing Township, NJ in 1961.

explanation: It joined a General Motors plant in New Jersey in 1961, lifting hot metal parts from a die-casting machine, a job too dangerous for people.

question: Boston Dynamics, maker of the Spot robot dog and the Atlas humanoid, has changed hands several times, including a spell under Google. Which car company owns it today?
topic: Robots, AI and the future of technology
source_excerpt: Hyundai Motor Group Completes Acquisition of Boston Dynamics from SoftBank

extra.why_interesting: Players know the viral robot videos and probably the Google link, but the current owner being a Korean carmaker is a genuine reveal.
extra.verification_notes: Hyundai Motor Group controls Boston Dynamics and in July 2026 moved to take full ownership by buying SoftBank's remaining stake, so the answer still holds.

explanation: Hyundai Motor Group bought a controlling stake from Japan's SoftBank in 2021, betting that factory robots and walking machines belong next to cars.

question: True or false: Deep Blue, the IBM computer that beat world chess champion Garry Kasparov in 1997, had lost a full match to him the year before.
topic: Robots, AI and the future of technology
source_excerpt: The first game of the 1996 match was the first game to be won by a chess-playing computer against a reigning world champion under normal chess tournament conditions.

extra.why_interesting: The 1997 defeat is famous; almost nobody remembers that the human champion had comfortably won round one the year before.
extra.verification_notes: Kasparov won the 1996 match 4–2 and Deep Blue won the 1997 rematch 3½–2½, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_Blue_versus_Garry_Kasparov

explanation: Kasparov won their first match in Philadelphia in 1996 by four games to two, and only the upgraded machine took the 1997 rematch.

question: In 1770 a chess-playing 'automaton' began touring Europe, beating challengers including Napoleon, until it was revealed that a human chess master was hidden inside. Amazon later borrowed its name for an online service where people do small tasks that computers cannot. What was the machine called?
topic: Robots, AI and the future of technology
source_excerpt: completed in early 1770 and first displayed in 1770 at Schönbrunn Palace; In 1809, Napoleon I played the Turk

extra.why_interesting: Players picture the first 'thinking machine' as a modern computer; the surprise is that an 18th-century box fooled emperors for decades because the intelligence was a hidden human, and Amazon knowingly named a service after that trick.
extra.verification_notes: Core fact is correct (Mechanical Turk, von Kempelen, 1770 debut, Napoleon 1809, Amazon MTurk namesake); only the tour start date (1783) is loosely phrased, but no alternative answer exists.

explanation: The figure at the board wore Ottoman robes and a turban, which gave the hoax its name, and Amazon chose it because its marketplace is likewise human intelligence disguised as a machine.

question: Long before it meant a handheld gadget, the word 'camera' was Latin for what kind of place that early artists actually stood inside?
source_excerpt: The term 'camera obscura' comes from Latin, meaning 'dark chamber.' The word 'camera' simply refers to a chamber or room, while 'obscura' means dark.

extra.why_interesting: Players use the word daily without noticing it originally described a whole room you could stand inside, not a gadget you hold.
extra.verification_notes: Latin 'camera' means chamber/room, and 'camera obscura' is the 'dark chamber' that artists worked in; the only quibble is that 'dark' comes from 'obscura' rather than 'camera' itself (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camera_obscura).

explanation: The camera obscura was a darkened chamber with a tiny hole in one wall, projecting the outside scene upside-down onto the opposite wall for artists to trace.

question: Which pair of French brothers charged the first paying audience to watch moving pictures, in a Paris café basement in December 1895?
source_excerpt: their first paid public screening

extra.why_interesting: A well-made classic: the birth of paying cinema audiences happened in a café basement, not a grand theatre.
extra.verification_notes: The Lumières' 28 Dec 1895 paid screening at the Grand Café is the traditional 'birth of cinema'. The Skladanowskys' earlier Berlin paid shows in Nov 1895 are a caveat, but the question's 'French', 'Paris' and 'café' constraints point only to the Lumières. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lumi%C3%A8re_brothers

explanation: Auguste and Louis Lumière showed ten short films to about thirty paying guests at the Grand Café, and the cinema business was born.

question: Apollo astronauts brought home only the film magazines and deliberately abandoned a dozen camera bodies on the Moon to save weight for rock samples. Which Swedish camera maker built them?
source_excerpt: from Apollo 11 to the final Apollo 17 mission, a total of twelve camera bodies were left behind on the lunar surface.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume the Moon cameras are museum pieces; in fact a dozen of them are still lying on the Moon, abandoned on purpose.
extra.verification_notes: Hasselblad's official history confirms twelve camera bodies were left on the Moon with only the film magazines returned; a Wikipedia count of 11 is a minor discrepancy that 'a dozen' as approximation tolerates.

explanation: Twelve Hasselblad bodies are still lying on the lunar surface, since every kilogram saved meant another kilogram of Moon rock could come back.

question: The dizzying camera trick where the background seems to stretch away while the actor stays the same size was invented for a 1958 Hitchcock film about a detective with a fear of heights. Which film?
source_excerpt: The dolly zoom was first created for Alfred Hitchcock's Vertigo; Irmin Roberts, a Paramount second-unit cameraman, devised the technique.

extra.why_interesting: Players have seen the dizzying stretch effect in Jaws and countless films; the stem's description of a fear of heights gives a deductive path to the 1958 original.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia's Dolly zoom article credits Irmin Roberts with creating the dolly zoom for Hitchcock's Vertigo (1958), with no earlier use noted.

explanation: The crew moved the camera backwards while zooming in, and the shot is still called the Vertigo effect, later borrowed by Spielberg for Jaws.

question: Which camera-stabilising rig, worn on the operator's body and invented by Garrett Brown, made possible the gliding shots that follow a boy's tricycle through the hotel corridors in The Shining?
source_excerpt: director Stanley Kubrick requested that the camera shoot from barely above the floor. This necessitated the invention of 'low mode'

extra.why_interesting: Players remember the gliding tricycle shot but rarely know it was made possible by a then-brand-new piece of gear with a name an interested adult can reach.
extra.verification_notes: Steadicam was invented by Garrett Brown and used on The Shining, including low-mode shots near floor level for the tricycle sequences; no newer developments affect this.

explanation: Brown's invention isolates the camera from the operator's footsteps, and he operated it himself for Kubrick, sometimes from a wheelchair to get the camera down to tricycle height.

question: In 1943, after a family photo on holiday, Edwin Land's three-year-old daughter asked him a question that led directly to the Polaroid instant camera. What did she want to know?
correct_answer: Why can't I see it now
alternative_answers: Why she couldn't see the photo right away
Why can't I see the picture
Why she had to wait to see it
Why the photo wasn't ready immediately
source_excerpt: his three-year-old eldest daughter, Jennifer... asked why she could not see the picture her father just took of her.

extra.why_interesting: A world-changing product came from a toddler's impatient question, and the stem gives enough footholds for the player to reason out exactly what she asked.
extra.verification_notes: Widely documented that in 1943 in Santa Fe, Land's 3-year-old daughter Jennifer asked why she couldn't see the photo right away; no later developments contradict it (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_H._Land).

explanation: Film then took days to develop, so Land spent the walk back working out the chemistry, and the first Polaroid camera went on sale five years later.

question: Before it filmed skydivers and mountain bikers, GoPro's very first product was a 35mm film camera on a wrist strap, built by its founder for which sport he loved?
source_excerpt: motivated by a 2002 surfing trip to Australia, in which he was hoping to capture high-quality action photos

extra.why_interesting: Players associate the brand with skiing, skydiving and mountain bikes, and few know its very first product was a film camera strapped to a surfer's wrist.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms GoPro's first product was a 35mm film wrist camera (2005) inspired by Nick Woodman's surfing trip to Australia.

explanation: Nick Woodman dreamed it up on a surf trip in 2002 because no camera let surfers photograph themselves on the wave, and the name means going professional with your shots.

question: Peter Jackson shot The Hobbit films at exactly double the frame rate cinema has used since the sound era. How many frames per second was that?
source_excerpt: used a filming and projection frame rate of 48 frames per second

extra.why_interesting: The player must know the long-standing cinema rate and double it; the payoff is that audiences found the smoother image looked oddly like television.
extra.verification_notes: The Hobbit trilogy was shot at 48 fps, exactly double the 24 fps standard since the sound era (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/high_frame_rate).

explanation: Film has run at 24 frames a second since the late 1920s, and many viewers found the smoother 48-frame look so unfamiliar that it reminded them of daytime television.

question: The oldest surviving photograph, a blurry view from a French farmhouse window by Nicéphore Niépce, was made in which decade?
source_excerpt: the oldest surviving photograph... made between June 4 and July 18, 1827, by Nicéphore Niépce

extra.why_interesting: Players anchor photography to the Daguerreotype of 1839 or the Victorian era, and are surprised the oldest surviving photo predates the first railways' heyday.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia dates View from the Window at Le Gras to 1827 (earlier estimate 1826), both in the 1820s, and calls it the oldest surviving photograph.

explanation: Niépce captured the view from his window at Le Gras in 1826 or 1827, more than a decade before his former partner Daguerre announced photography to the world.

question: The original 2007 iPhone had a rear camera with no flash, no autofocus and no video mode. How many megapixels did it have?
source_excerpt: 2.0 MP with geotagging (not GPS-based)

extra.why_interesting: Today's phones advertise 48 or 200 megapixels; players assume the original iPhone was at least in the single-digit range above its true, tiny figure.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia lists the original iPhone's rear camera as 2.0 MP; the no-flash, no-autofocus and no-video claims come from general knowledge, not from that page.

explanation: Two megapixels was behind many ordinary phones of the time, and it took until the iPhone 3GS two years later before an iPhone could record video at all.

question: The 1939 Wizard of Oz got its glorious colour from a Technicolor camera that exposed three strips of film at once, each through a different coloured filter. What kind of film stock were those three strips?
source_excerpt: The beam splitter allowed one-third of the light coming through the camera lens to pass through the reflector and a green filter and form an image on one of the strips

extra.why_interesting: The most famous early colour film in history never had a single frame of colour film inside the camera.
extra.verification_notes: Three-strip Technicolor cameras used three black-and-white negatives behind a beam splitter and colour filters, with colour added only at the dye-transfer printing stage (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technicolor).

explanation: Each strip recorded only one colour component as shades of grey, and the three were combined into a colour print afterwards.

question: In 1975 a Kodak engineer built the first digital camera, a 3.6 kilogram box that needed 23 seconds to save each picture. Onto what everyday 1970s storage medium did it record the image?
source_excerpt: 8 pounds (3.6 kg)... twenty-three seconds per image... cassette tape

extra.why_interesting: Players picture floppy disks or memory chips; the foothold is the year, which points to the dominant portable medium of the time, and the answer feels right once heard.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Sasson's 1975 prototype weighed 3.6 kg, took 23 seconds per image, and recorded to cassette tape.

explanation: Steven Sasson's prototype wrote a 100 by 100 pixel image to an audio-style cassette, and playback needed a special reader connected to a television.
